tier_reason: Peer-reviewed OSDI'14 paper (Bangert & Zeldovich). The published text names an Intel i7-3610QM (one core, 12GB RAM), and the repo ships the benchmark code (examples/dns/bench: random-domains.rb, queryperf, results.50000/all.qps) plus -std=gnu99 -O3 in examples/dns/Makefile. It is not A because the C compiler is never named (make's default CC) and BIND's build is not described.

corrections.claimed_speedup: median throughput ~139,215 qps (NailDNS) vs ~47,234 qps (BIND 9.9.5 per the paper text; the figure caption says 9.5.5), ~2.9x faster (derived from page data); median round-trip time 0.139 ms vs 0.416 ms (derived from page data, box plot of 7 runs each)
corrections.workload: Authoritative-DNS load test. 50,000 random dictionary-based domains (com/net/org), ~90% of them written to the zone file, so ~10% of queries get NXDOMAIN. Each domain is queried 0-3 times (per the paper) in shuffled order with BIND's queryperf, at most 20 outstanding queries, for 60 s. 7 runs with a daemon restart between runs, against ISC BIND 9.9.5 on the same local machine, one core.
corrections.hardware: Intel i7-3610QM, single core, 12GB RAM (OSDI'14 paper, Performance subsection)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: NailDNS C server built with -std=gnu99 -O3 (examples/dns/Makefile); compiler not named (make default CC); BIND 9.9.5 build flags not stated
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed OSDI'14 paper (USENIX, MIT CSAIL authors). The paper states the CPU (i7-3610QM, one core) and the repo ships the benchmark scripts, queryperf and raw results (examples/dns/bench), but the C compiler and BIND's build are unstated, so the tier is B, not A. The paper body says BIND 9.9.5 (2014), but the figure caption says 9.5.5, probably a caption typo. NailDNS is a minimal 183-line demo server that lacks many BIND features, and the test ran over loopback on one machine. Last commit was 2015 (abandoned).

notes: The record said no CPU model is stated anywhere and that the baseline is BIND 9.5.5 from 2009. In fact the published paper and eval.tex state an i7-3610QM and BIND 9.9.5; both are corrected. The record's last_commit 2020-07-27 was the repo's pushed_at date: the only branch (master) last committed on 2015-08-17. Usability is changed to copyable per the MIT-license rule, and the demo-server nature is kept in caveats. The medians were re-derived from the fig-perf-dns data, which matches results.50000/all.qps.

tier_reason: latest-results.md has picoquic and quiche rows with the cited p50s (upload syscall 15.823 vs 14.794 Gbps; connect syscall 297 vs 277 conn/s; all four rows publishable), and pairwise-comparisons.tsv confirms them (upload 1.070 [CI 1.061-1.076], connect 1.071 [1.049-1.095]). The harness code (perf.picoquic.h, perf.quiche.h, depofiles/) and flags are public, but no CPU model is recorded. quicperf is also a small personal harness (27 stars) whose author contributes to picoquic, so it is neither A nor B; this is the same C ruling batch 22 gave ngtcp2 and TQUIC on this harness.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ~1.06-1.07x quiche on bulk upload and connection setup (p50, derived from page data): upload syscall 15.823 vs 14.794 Gbps (1.07x; pairwise 95% CI 1.061-1.076), upload io_uring 14.549 vs 13.755 Gbps (1.06x), connect syscall 297 vs 277 conn/s (1.07x; CI 1.049-1.095). In the same run picoquic is slower than quiche in the other 18 of 21 publishable pairwise comparisons, all syscall: request/response 59,098 vs 64,574 rps (0.92x), flow control 0.94x, loss recovery 7.590 vs 11.689 Gbps (0.65x), small-payload messages 0.67x, close/reset 0.66x, 0-RTT 0.86x, multistream download 0.546 vs 10.990 Gbps (0.05x) and multistream upload 0.591 vs 15.291 Gbps (0.04x). Its bidirectional (0.22 vs 12.66 Gbps) and DATAGRAM rows are inconclusive.
corrections.workload: quicperf loopback harness: Linux, C++-owned UDP I/O shared by all stacks, CUBIC, shared TLS 1.3 Ed25519 material, one pinned server thread. Upload is client-to-server bulk transfer (8-byte request plus bulk body, duration mode) on the syscall backend. picoquic ran with 2 client threads and quiche with 4; a saturation scout chose each library's thread count. Each row has 20 samples in 5 randomized blocks, and both rows are publishable. Also Connect (full handshake plus bidi stream creation, at most 128 handshakes per sample), syscall, 16 client threads each.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: quicperf C++ harness: CMake Release, C++20, -O3 -march=native, LTO (CMakeLists.txt, README); exact compiler/version not published. picoquic pinned at master commit 2b1e14d (2026-05-16) with picotls 7c32032 (fusion on) and OpenSSL 4.0.0 via depofiles/picoquic.DepoFile. quiche 0.29.0 (e85fc8e) built with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native -C opt-level=3', fat LTO, codegen-units=1.
corrections.caveats: quicperf (victorstewart/quicperf, 27 stars) is a small personal harness, not a well-known suite. Its author has 57 commits in private-octopus/picoquic, so the harness is not fully independent for this pair. docs/results/fixed-full-matrix-max16-20260601T175816Z/fixed-environment.txt records only an anonymized machine_hash (no CPU model). The 2026-06-01 run came from a dirty working tree, with uncommitted edits to perf.picoquic.h, perf.quiche.h and other adapters on commit 3eda036. Loopback only. The wins are narrow: ~6-7% on upload (both backends) and on syscall connect, and connect rates for all 12 stacks cluster at 234-306 conn/s. picoquic loses to quiche in 18 of 21 publishable pairwise comparisons, by 16-26x on multistream transfers.

notes: The numbers and row ownership check out (both cited rows publishable), but quiche's Upload row used 4 client threads, not 2; corrected in workload. Downgraded B to C to match batch 22's quicperf ruling (obscure harness, no CPU model). claimed_speedup now discloses that picoquic is slower than quiche on most quicperf scenarios. Metadata checks out: MIT, 776 stars, last commit 2026-09-25, active, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: latest-results.md has the cited Connect rows (quic-zig syscall 286 vs quiche syscall 277 conn/s p50, both publishable), and pairwise-comparisons.tsv confirms the edge (quiche/quic-zig 0.968, CI 0.961-0.990). The harness code and flags are public, but no CPU model is recorded, and quicperf is a small personal harness (27 stars). That makes it tier C, not A or B, matching batch 22's ruling on this harness.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Connect only: 286 vs 277 conn/s p50 syscall (1.03x, derived from page data; pairwise quiche/quic-zig 0.968, CI 0.961-0.990) and 267 vs 258 conn/s io_uring (1.03x). In the same run quic-zig is slower than quiche in the other 21 of 23 publishable pairwise comparisons, all syscall unless noted: upload 10.642 vs 14.794 Gbps (0.72x), flow control 0.82x, multistream download 3.166 vs 10.990 Gbps (0.29x), request/response 3,704 vs 64,574 rps (~17x slower), and ~13-20x slower on stream churn, small-payload messages, 0-RTT and close/reset. Resumed connect is 14.6 vs 305.9 conn/s (~21x slower, io_uring). Idle footprint is ~3.7x larger (464,384 vs 125,440 bytes/connection, inconclusive row).
corrections.workload: quicperf loopback harness: Connect scenario (full handshake plus bidirectional stream creation, count mode capped at 128 handshakes per sample), CUBIC, shared TLS 1.3 Ed25519 material, syscall backend. quic-zig ran with 8 client threads and quiche with 16; a saturation scout chose each library's thread count. Each row has 20 samples in 5 randomized blocks, and both rows are publishable. quic-zig runs as a Zig packet engine behind the harness's C++-owned UDP I/O.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: quic-zig built from the fork victorstewart/quic-zig at commit 97a7bec (quicperf-tls-wall-clock, 2026-05-18) via depofiles/quiczig.DepoFile, with zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native; CMakeLists.txt hints Zig 0.16.0 x86_64-linux. The C++ harness is C++20 -O3 -march=native with LTO. quiche 0.29.0 was built with -C target-cpu=native -C opt-level=3 and fat LTO. The exact C++ compiler is not published.
corrections.caveats: quicperf (victorstewart/quicperf, 27 stars) is a small personal harness. It records no CPU model (machine_hash only), and the 2026-06-01 run came from a dirty working tree. It benchmarks a fork commit of quic-zig (victorstewart/quic-zig 97a7bec, which switches TLS certificate validity to wall clock), not upstream endel/quic-zig. The only win is ~3% on Connect, where all 12 stacks cluster at 234-306 conn/s. quic-zig is slower than quiche in 21 of 23 publishable pairwise comparisons, by up to ~21x. quic-zig's own README makes no performance claims.

notes: Rejected as not-faster. The row numbers are accurate, but the lone ~3% Connect edge (a harness-clustered metric) sits among 21 losses to quiche, 13-21x on request, stream and resumption workloads, and the project does not claim to be faster. quiche's Connect row used 16 client threads, not 8. If the entry is kept under the keep-and-document policy, use the corrected fields at tier C. Metadata checks out: MIT, 57 stars, last commit 2026-09-25, active, not a fork.
